summary: Grafton County, NH: a Black Mountain (Benton) lookout site from 1911; the discontinued lookout was destroyed in 1978, and no source describes the summit today.

facts.design: CT-2 timber tower with L-4 type cab (1941)
facts.status_note: Discontinued and destroyed in 1978; no source describes what remains on the summit
facts.agency: White Mountain National Forest; the NH Forestry department ran the tower until 1939

access.note: The summit is in the White Mountain National Forest; the hiking route starts at Howe Hill Road in Benton

visit.trail_note: Black Mountain Trail from the trailhead on Howe Hill Road in Benton; there is no tower to climb

events.note: Site first established as an observation point
New and improved watch tower in the 1915-1916 biennium
Steel tower with a wooden house on top erected in the 1926 season, replacing an older wooden observation tower
Herbert L. Beamis had been the watchman for four years
Lightning melted about 2,000 feet of telephone line and cut off the station; the tower was not damaged
Damaged in the Great New England Hurricane
White Mountain National Forest took over operation of the tower from the state
28-foot CT-2 timber tower with an L-4 type cab constructed
Maud Bickford returned as the fire watcher; she held the job the year before

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The state forestry department ran the tower until the White Mountain National Forest took over operation in 1939; the record's agency is the later one.

notes_for_editor: The history is detailed and dated, but almost all of it comes from one compiled page of newspaper and report extracts (Forest Lookouts), so confidence is medium. The page does not say whether the 1941 timber tower replaced the 1926 steel tower or the 1926 tower stood until 1941; the story does not claim either. The record's L-4 design and 8.5 m height match the 1941 entry (28 feet). The summit height differs by source (Wikipedia gives 2,840 ft, the blog 2,836 ft, HikerNerd 2,830 ft) and is not in the facts. TrailsNH was blocked (403), so its 'no longer standing' note was not used. No source describes the summit today, so the story says so. Wikipedia places the state forest itself in Haverhill and does not name Benton; the summit's Benton location comes from the 1926 and 1939 reports and the trip report, so the story now cites the Forest Lookouts page for Benton as well.
